explanations.explanation: Asaph, the psalm's writer, says it plain: “But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped.” He could have stopped at the nice first line and left it there. Instead he tells on himself. I respect that, friend, because most of us would have kept the wobble off the record.

Not quite, friend. Asaph says the opposite: “my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped.” A man who says he almost slipped is a man who has felt the floor move. I think that's why this song feels so real.

explanations.answer: He had written his last song
explanations.explanation: No last song here, friend. Asaph is right in the middle of this one, and he's still singing. What he says is that his feet had almost stumbled and his steps had nearly slipped. He's telling us how close he came to falling.

Yes, “For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.” It's that feeling when you see somebody else's vacation pictures on a Monday morning, and you're sitting at your desk. Asaph doesn't dress it up. He just calls it envy.

Asaph doesn't pity them here. He says, “For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.” They looked like they were doing great, and that's what got to him. Pity would have been a much calmer song, friend.
No fear in this line, friend. The verse says, “For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.” He looked at their prosperity and wanted what they had. Envy is the word he chose.

That's it: “They are free of the burdens others carry; they are not afflicted like other men.” You know that person who carries all the bags in one trip and never even breathes hard? That's how Asaph sees them. Life's weight just seems to skip them.
Close, but the verse doesn't say blessings. Asaph says they are “free of the burdens others carry.” It's about what they don't have to carry, friend. He's looking at the load, not at the gifts.

Dreams don't come up in this verse, friend. Asaph says, “They are free of the burdens others carry; they are not afflicted like other men.” The word is burdens. He's watching people who seem to walk through life with empty hands.

Right, friend. Asaph says, “They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression.” When these folks open their mouths, nothing kind comes out. That's the part that stings the most.
Not here, friend. Asaph says, “They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression.” It's the opposite of thanks. Their words are aimed to hurt.
Nobody's hiding in this verse, friend. Asaph says, “They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression.” And the next verse gets even louder. These people are out in the open.

I get why it sounds possible, friend, but it's the other way around. Asaph says, “They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut across the earth.” Their talk doesn't leave heaven out. It goes right at it, and it goes everywhere on earth too.

Right, it's False. The verse says, “They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut across the earth.” Their big talk reaches up toward heaven and out across the earth. Nothing stays private with these folks, friend.

That's it. The wicked say, “How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?” They're not asking anything big about being forgiven or paid back. They're wondering whether He even knows what's going on. Asaph is quoting them here, friend, he's not agreeing with them.

Nobody here is asking for forgiveness, friend. The wicked say, “How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?” Their question is about whether God knows anything at all. Asking to be forgiven would be a very different song.
Repaying doesn't come up in their question, friend. They say, “How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?” It's all about whether God knows. Asaph is repeating what they say.

Yes, Asaph says, “Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands.” In vain means it felt like it was for nothing. He's looking at his clean hands and the wicked's easy life, and it's not adding up for him. I think we've all had a moment like that, friend.

Not in this verse, friend. Asaph says, “Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands.” Right now he's in the low point of the song. I think the worth part comes later, once he gets his bearings.

Asaph doesn't say it's too much to keep up, friend. He says, “Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands.” His complaint is that it's in vain. It isn't about being tired.
True. Asaph says, “For I am afflicted all day long and punished every morning.” That's the hard part for him. He kept his heart pure, and mornings still feel heavy. I think this one hurts, friend.

It's True, friend, and that's the sting of it. Asaph says, “For I am afflicted all day long and punished every morning.” He kept his heart pure, and he still feels this every morning. I think this is one of the heavier lines in the psalm.

Right. Asaph says, “If I had said, ‘I will speak this way,’ then I would have betrayed Your children.” He's got all these thoughts in his head, but he knows what talking that way would do. Some words are better kept in the oven until they're done, friend.

Friends don't come up here, friend. Asaph says, “If I had said, ‘I will speak this way,’ then I would have betrayed Your children.” The text names God's children, not a friend list. That's what he's worried about.
No king in this verse, friend. Asaph says, “If I had said, ‘I will speak this way,’ then I would have betrayed Your children.” The weight here is on God's children. A king never enters the picture.

That's the turn, friend. Asaph says it was troublesome “until I entered God’s sanctuary; then I discerned their end.” He didn't figure it out by staring harder at the problem. Something changed when he went into that place.

No palace in this song, friend. Asaph says it was troublesome “until I entered God’s sanctuary; then I discerned their end.” The turn happens in God's sanctuary. That's where things come into focus for him.
The city gate isn't mentioned, friend. Asaph says, “until I entered God’s sanctuary; then I discerned their end.” That's where the turn happens. Nothing else in the passage comes close to it.
Yes, Asaph says, “then I discerned their end.” He'd been staring at where the wicked were right now. In the sanctuary he saw where they were headed. That makes a big difference, friend.
Plans aren't in this verse, friend. Asaph says, “then I discerned their end.” He didn't read their plans. He saw where they end up.
He'd already seen plenty of their wealth, friend. That was the problem. What he sees in the sanctuary is new: “then I discerned their end.” It's their end, not their bank account.

True. Asaph says, “Surely You set them on slick ground; You cast them down into ruin.” It looked like solid ground from the outside. Now he sees it differently. Anybody who's hit a freshly mopped floor at full speed knows how that goes.

It's actually True, friend. Asaph says, “Surely You set them on slick ground; You cast them down into ruin.” What looked so steady to him in the first half of the song isn't steady at all. The sanctuary showed him the ground they're on.

Yes, “I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You.” Asaph looks back at his grieving time and doesn't go easy on himself. That's a man being honest, friend. I think that honesty is part of why the psalm works.
Not this time, friend. Asaph says, “I was senseless and ignorant.” He's not polishing his record here. He's telling it straight.
Patient isn't the word, friend. Asaph says, “I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You.” He doesn't call himself calm about any of it. He's looking back with total honesty.

I know why it feels like it could be, friend, but it's the other way around. Asaph says, “Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand.” After all that envy and confusion, God doesn't let go. His hand is still holding Asaph's.

That's right, it's False. Asaph says, “Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand.” That little word “yet” carries a lot. He messed up in his thinking, and he's still held. Friend, that's good news for all of us.
Yes, “You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory.” Notice what Asaph gets. It's not a pile of stuff, it's guidance. And there's more coming after that, friend.

explanations.answer: Makes him rich like the wicked
explanations.explanation: Money isn't in this verse, friend. Asaph says, “You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory.” What he gets is guidance and glory. He isn't asking for the wicked's lifestyle anymore.

explanations.answer: Gives him a life with no trouble
explanations.explanation: Asaph doesn't promise himself an easy life, friend. He says, “You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory.” A few verses later he even says, “My flesh and my heart may fail.” He has God's guidance, and that's what he holds on to.
That's the first blank. Asaph says, “My flesh and my heart may fail.” He's honest that he's not made of steel. Then he gets to the good part, friend, so keep going.

Yes, “but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.” Asaph's own heart may give out, but God doesn't. A portion is what is his, and he says it's God Himself. I'd take that over a big pile of cookie boxes, friend.
Prosper is the wicked's word in this psalm, friend, not Asaph's. He says, “My flesh and my heart may fail.” He's admitting he can give out. Prosperity isn't what he's counting on anymore.

Burden shows up earlier in the psalm, friend, when Asaph says the wicked are free of the burdens others carry. In this verse the word for God is different: “God is the strength of my heart.” He's not calling God a burden. He's calling Him strength.

Worry isn't in this verse, friend. Asaph says, “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.” He doesn't say God is a worry. He says God is his strength and his portion.

explanations.answer: It is good to draw near to God
explanations.explanation: That's where he lands. Asaph says, “But as for me, it is good to draw near to God.” Remember, at the start he was staring at what the wicked had. Now he's looking at who he has. That's quite the turn, friend.

explanations.answer: It is good to have great wealth
explanations.explanation: Wealth is what Asaph envied at the start, friend. By the end he says, “But as for me, it is good to draw near to God.” His eyes have moved. He's not chasing the wicked's life anymore.

explanations.answer: It is good to make a great name
explanations.explanation: A great name doesn't show up in this psalm, friend. Asaph's last words are, “But as for me, it is good to draw near to God.” That's the good thing he lands on. The search ends with God, not with a name.
